thesis: Vancouver in July is when the geography it is famous for becomes part of daily life.
scene: It's 8:40 in the evening and still fully light. At Kitsilano Beach the volleyball courts are going and will keep going for another hour. Somebody has brought a paddleboard on a bicycle. The North Shore mountains are sitting above the far side of the water with snow still on the tops, close enough to look like a backdrop someone installed. A group has been in the same spot since five and shows no sign of packing up; one of them is still in a wetsuit, dry now, not bothering to change. Office clothes are visible in the crowd. Nobody went home first.

sceneAnchors.text: The western end of the string of beaches, where the driftwood logs function as assigned seating nobody assigned. People swim, then sit on a log facing north-west and stay there until the light goes, which in July is close to ten. The city is directly behind them and briefly irrelevant.

The continuous path around the edge of the downtown peninsula, used all year and used differently in July. After six it fills with people who are commuting and people who are not, at the same speed, and the distinction stops being visible. Bike traffic has its own etiquette that nobody explains to you.

The small lake in East Vancouver with a Saturday farmers market and a dog beach, where the crowd is entirely people who live within a few blocks. In July the field around it is occupied from late afternoon onward by groups who arrived separately. Nothing about it is scenic. It is the most used park in the city.

locals: Work ends and people go directly to water. Not home first — directly, with a towel in a bag that has been in the bag since June. Swimming happens after dinner because it is still warm and still light. The mountains get mentioned constantly, in the specific phrase used when they are visible, and the phrase carries relief rather than pride. Weekends are decided by whether the forecast holds, and if it holds nobody stays inside, because everybody knows how few of these weeks there are.

localWord.translation: said on the clear days when the North Shore is visible
localWord.body: Not a joke, and not about the view. The mountains arrive and depart with the cloud. In July they stay, and the city stops being a place with weather over it.

changes: The setting stops being scenery and starts being infrastructure. The water is somewhere you go after work, not somewhere you photograph. You begin to understand that the eight months of grey are the reason July is used this hard, and that the intensity you are seeing is not enthusiasm but accounting.
start: Carrying a towel every day. Leaving work at a time that would be early anywhere else and finding it is normal here in July. You start swimming in water that is colder than it looks and stopping caring after the first minute. You learn which beach the sun sets behind and go to that one. Evenings extend past nine without anyone deciding to extend them.
stop: Saving the good weather for something. There is no better day coming that this one is being held for. Vancouver in July operates on the understanding that the sun is spending down a balance, and the correct response to a clear Tuesday is to go outside on the Tuesday.
returns: Light, in quantities that feel like an error. And the specific pleasure of a city that is briefly, completely aligned with where it was built — mountains visible, water warm enough, everyone outside at once. It does not last, and the fact that it does not last is why it works.
remember: The mountains were always there. July is when the city can see them.

items.label: February
items.body: Everything is grey and low, and the mountains stay behind cloud.

items.label: July
items.body: The mountains are out, the water is warm, and the evenings run past nine.

items.label: October
items.body: The rains arrive and the mountains disappear for months.
